summary:
Labuan is a federal territory of Malaysia and stands under the Malaysian national framework: sections 377A and 377B of the Penal Code 1936 criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of gross indecency, carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping. The provisions apply to any person regardless of gender or consent, are not confined to Malaysian nationals, and therefore reach foreign visitors in Labuan.

The Sharia layer that criminalises cross-dressing and "a man posing as a woman" applies to Muslims only, and a dual court system places Muslims under Sharia jurisdiction while the federal courts handle Penal Code offences. A non-Muslim foreign visitor therefore falls outside the Sharia offences; the federal provisions, which carry the heavier penalties and apply to everyone, are the operative exposure.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded in the Malaysian framework, so a trans visitor cannot obtain documents matching their gender here. No federal law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no same-sex marriage or recognition of same-sex partners.

Enforcement documented since the 2018 election is raid-based rather than directed at individual stops: an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur produced arrests of at least 20 LGBT people, and an August raid on an LGBT venue detained twenty men. A Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned, and in November 2023 Johor state authorities announced plans for conversion-therapy centres.

Human Rights Watch, with Justice For Sisters, interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021, documenting state-backed discrimination, harassment of LGBT activists and organisations, and raids on private events, alongside a federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison.

Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had drawn at least 1,733 attendees by June 2021. Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported in the country, with transgender people particularly vulnerable.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor in Labuan, the practical exposure is the federal Penal Code and the pattern of venue-and-event raids with public outing, not Sharia jurisdiction. The sources reviewed record no Labuan-specific enforcement case and no documented targeting of foreign tourists.
tangentialFactors:
Queue-and-venue operations carry acute exposure for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in the Chow Kit area of Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were published; 17 civil servants identified among those held were suspended. A magistrate rejected the extension of remand for lack of ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point, among them 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. A legal-aid organisation mobilised bailors and counsel. On 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Litigation has narrowed the state Sharia layer without loosening the federal one. A High Court request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional was refused, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014, filed after 16 trans women were arrested at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Official hostility has been stated in explicit terms. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his full licence to carry out enforcement actions against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists called on him to revoke. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised over a charge of insulting Islam before she fled the country and received UNHCR protection.

Trans-specific lethal violence is documented alongside official indifference. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The surrounding climate constrains any expectation of change: Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, and LGBT events and media content are censored. Compared with jurisdictions that provide legal gender recognition and hate-crime protection, Malaysia offers neither, so a trans visitor cannot rely on enhanced sentencing or on document remedies if they are harassed.
localsOnly:
Residents who are Muslim are subject to Sharia jurisdiction in a dual court system, and every one of the 13 states plus the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men.

Enforcement of those enactments is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing, leaving the offence at officer discretion. Residents who are not Muslim fall outside the Sharia offences but remain exposed to the Penal Code.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable, so residents live without corrected identity documents, and no federal law protects them against discrimination in employment, housing, services or education on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, which affects inheritance, hospital visitation and next-of-kin decisions.

Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and in November 2023 Johor state authorities announced plans for conversion-therapy centres. LGBT events and media content are censored, and state religious authorities have harassed LGBT activists and organisations and raided private gatherings.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Labuan's own Sharia enactment contains a cross-dressing or anti-trans provision is unresolved in the sources reviewed. The inventory records such enactments across all 13 states and expressly for the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, and does not extend that listing to Labuan; the Human Rights Watch federal-territory finding is stated for Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya only. No source consulted states that the parent federal Sharia framework applies here.

No Labuan-specific enforcement case, arrest, raid or prosecution appears in the audited sources, so the enforcement picture for the territory is inferred from nationally applicable provisions rather than observed locally.

Not sourced: entry and visa screening practice for trans travellers, including whether immigration officers inspect gender markers against presentation, and whether Malaysian authorities permit entry with documents amended abroad. Also unsourced: facility access rules for gendered toilets and security screening, access to hormone therapy or HIV care for visitors, and any consular guidance specific to detention of trans nationals.

The criminal penalties quoted are statutory maxima; the sources do not give Labuan-specific conviction rates or sentencing practice, and the frequency of enforcement against consenting adults in private is not quantified for this territory.
